title: Heart Attack Patients Had More Microplastics in Their Blood, Study Finds
excerpt: A study of 61 Italian patients found microplastics in the blood of 84 percent of heart attack patients — along with higher inflammatory markers — but researchers caution it does not prove causation.
body:
• Microplastics and nanoplastics were detected in the blood of 84 percent of heart attack patients, versus 40 percent of patients with chronic heart disease and 32 percent of those with healthy arteries.
  • Patients with more plastic particles also showed elevated inflammatory markers TNF-α and interleukin-6.
  • Smokers were six times more likely to have microplastics in their blood; every patient who smoked and had high pollution exposure had plastics in their blood.
  • The researchers stress the findings show a strong association, not proof that microplastics cause heart attacks.

Patients suffering heart attacks had significantly more microplastics and nanoplastics in their blood than people with chronic heart disease or healthy coronary arteries, according to a study published this month in the European Heart Journal.

The study, conducted at Sant'Andrea University Hospital and the Azienda Ospedaliera Universitaria Integrata of Verona in Italy, examined 61 adults, including 19 experiencing ST-elevation myocardial infarctions. Researchers collected blood samples from vessels supplying the heart and from limbs, and estimated air pollution exposure from patients' home addresses. Microplastics and nanoplastics — plastic fragments smaller than 5 millimeters and 1 micrometer respectively — were detected in 84 percent of the heart attack patients, who also carried a broader array of plastic types than the other groups. Polyethylene, the plastic common in packaging and consumer products, was the most frequent type.

"These findings do not prove that microplastics cause heart attacks, but they reveal a strong association between environmental exposures, microplastics in the blood and cardiovascular disease."

— Prof Emanuele Barbato, Sapienza University of Rome

Context & Background

Microplastics are now found in virtually every environmental compartment — air, water, soil — and increasingly inside the human body, including blood, lung tissue, placenta, and breast milk, according to an accompanying editorial by Prof Andreas Daiber of the University Medical Centre Mainz. People ingest or inhale the particles, but previous evidence on their health risks was inconclusive, and little was known about whether the particles are present in coronary circulation — the blood flowing through the arteries that supply the heart.

The new findings build on a landmark 2024 study linking microplastics in carotid artery plaque to a higher risk of cardiovascular events and death. "As each study emerges showing a potential link," cardiologist Dr Sean Mendez of Weill Cornell Medicine and NewYork-Presbyterian Hospital, who was not involved in the research, told Health.com, "the urgency for understanding the cardiovascular and overall health implications becomes larger."

Impact & Analysis

The study's strongest signals concern how the particles may get into the bloodstream. Samples with more microplastics also showed elevated tumor necrosis factor α (TNF-α) and interleukin-6, suggesting an inflammatory response. Smoking history was the most powerful predictor: smokers were six times more likely to have microplastics in their blood, and every patient who smoked and had higher long-term air pollution exposure had plastics in their blood, compared with just 12.5 percent of non-smokers with lower pollution exposure. The researchers suggest smoking may make it easier for micro- and nanoplastics to enter the bloodstream via the lungs, with air pollution acting in a similar way.

But the authors are careful about the limits: the study included only 61 patients, cannot establish direction of causation — heart attacks themselves could conceivably alter blood composition — and environmental exposure estimates are indirect. Policies that reduce air pollution, tobacco exposure, and plastic contamination, Prof Barbato said, could have benefits for cardiovascular health alongside environmental ones, but the microplastic-heart disease link remains an association awaiting mechanistic proof.

Diaspora Angle

The smoking and air-pollution links give the findings particular resonance in regions where both exposures run high; for readers in heavily polluted cities, the study adds one more reason to treat clean air and tobacco avoidance as cardiovascular priorities.

What's Next

Researchers say larger studies and mechanistic work are needed to determine whether plastic particles actively drive vascular inflammation and clotting, or merely ride along with the exposures that do. Until then, the finding joins a growing body of evidence that the bloodstream carries plastic fragments throughout the body — and that what is in the air and water may increasingly show up in the heart.
